extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, history, and constitutional design; policymakers interested in republican institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating institutional principles for stable republican government (checks and balances, legislative structure, public education, rule of law) as illustrated by ancient Greek and Roman examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three orders / checks and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nothing has ever effected it but three different orders of men, bound by their interests to watch over each other, and stand the guardians of the laws."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that orders of men watching and balancing each other are the only security against arbitrary magistrates and popular turbulence; gives ancient examples (Crotona, Rome) showing failure where such balances were lacking or broken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power must be opposed to power; interest to interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "Power must be opposed to power, and interest to interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that institutional equilibrium arises from countervailing forces rather than from education or religion alone; used to justify structural checks rather than reliance on moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and religion alone are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Education, religion, aristocracy, democracy, and monarchy, singly, are totally inadequate to restrain the passions of men, preserve steady government, and protect lives, liberties, and properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly warns that moral education and religious sentiment cannot substitute for structural checks; historical anecdotes (Pythagoreans, Sybaris) illustrate collapse despite moral/religious efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong independent executive in a single person
rubrics_metrics.description: "The necessity of a strong and independent executive in a single person..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an English improvement unknown (or not practiced) by the ancients; argued necessary to effective government when paired with appropriate legislative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three branches in the legislature and equality among them
rubrics_metrics.description: "The necessity ... of three branches in the legislature instead of two, and of an equality among the three."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims English institutional innovation of three balanced branches better restrains abuse than two-branch systems; supports design that prevents any two parts from dominating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty and publicity of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a miserable servitude... where the law is uncertain and unknown; and it is only under the security of certain and known laws, that arts, sciences, agriculture, commerce, and trades can ever be made to flourish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, known laws are essential for social prosperity; uncertainty produces servitude and stifles economic and intellectual life—presented as a core desideratum for constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury as a vital institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The text praises trial by jury (noting Solon's institution) as a significant advance toward civilization and legal fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial by jury singled out among ancient legal advances; implied criterion for evaluating legal systems' fairness and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public education for literacy under public expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Charondas ordained that all the sons of every family should learn to write and read under masters in the pay of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a law of high merit deserving imitation by free peoples; public schooling for basic literacy is framed as a foundational civic good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates must be impartial and modest
rubrics_metrics.description: "The chiefs of his republics ought not to govern with arrogance nor pride; nor should the magistrates be guided in their judgments by hatred nor by friendship."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zaleucus's preamble sets impartiality and modesty of magistrates as criteria; guides against factional/judicial partiality and personal bias in officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should promote reconciliation and forbid irreconcilable enmity
rubrics_metrics.description: Zaleucus ordained that there should never be any irreconcilable enmity among citizens; animosities should be only a passage to sincere reconciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should include norms or mechanisms that encourage reconciliation and social cohesion, viewing persistent enmity as 'savage' in civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/pious preamble to the laws to ground morals
rubrics_metrics.description: Zaleucus's preamble declares inhabitants ought to be persuaded there is a God and to adore the gods as authors of good and beautiful, holding souls pure because gods accept only just and beneficent actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using religious language in a preamble is justified as a way to fix attention on piety and wisdom and to ground laws in a philosophical/rational conception of duty and honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the law over ad hoc mercy: limit innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: Charondas forbade proposals of changes in his laws; his principle: 'Whether you shall save the law or the criminal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes legal stability and the supremacy of the law over individual pleas or rhetorical substitutions; presented as a means to control democratic disorder but also criticized by historical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe social punishments to deter slander/calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: Charondas ordained that all who should be convicted of calumny should be conducted through the streets crowned with tamarin (an infamous punishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of harsh public-shaming penalties intended to deter defamation; noted as so infamous that some preferred death—used to illustrate extreme legislative methods to enforce social decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of association with wicked men to prevent moral contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Charondas prohibited all society with wicked men, reasoning that many initially loving virtue are drawn by secret seductions to greater vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law prescribing social limitations as preventive of moral corruption; presented as a preventive public-morality rule within Charondas's code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for guardianship of orphans (property vs education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Property of orphans to be administered by the relations by the father; their persons and education entrusted to those by the mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific allocation of guardianship roles illustrates that family- and gender-based divisions of responsibility were legislated; included as a criterion of social order and child welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of civic duty by public humiliation for draft evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: All those who should refuse to take arms for their country, or quit their ranks, instead of death, should be exposed three days in a public square of the city in women's clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of ritualized humiliation to enforce military/civic duty; presented as an alternative punitive regime to death, aimed at social pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections and sacrosanctity for popular representatives (tribunes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunes' persons were made sacred; an oath protected them from being struck—those who harmed them were devoted to infernal gods; this sacrosanctity enabled tribunes to interrupt the senate and advocate for the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional protections for representatives are presented as necessary to empower popular magistrates against aristocratic obstruction; sacralization used tactically to secure political function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish hereditary distinctions; open offices by merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The divine original of nobility and exclusion of plebeians from office is criticized; reform aimed to remove disqualification of plebeian birth and allow access by merit and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing hereditary barriers and enabling merit-based officeholding is set as a constitutional criterion to correct aristocratic monopoly and improve justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly assign jurisdictions among assemblies to avoid constitutional contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty about what business should be done in one assembly or another (centuries vs tribes) produced continual altercations and contradictions that undermined government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should specify competences of different assemblies to avoid overlap and persistent conflict; ambiguity invites demagogues and institutional breakdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant negative/veto powers to executive or appropriate organs to balance senate and people
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues that if consuls had possessed a negative in the legislature and all the executive authority, and the senate and people had been made equal and independent, the republic might have endured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests institutionalizing veto/negative powers as a balancing mechanism between competing bodies; used to explain Roman crises and propose design remedies.
